query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys under tribo-corrosion conditions, the overall degradation is governed by a cyclic process in which controlled sliding wear intermittently removes the native passive oxide film, exposing the underlying metal to accelerated corrosion, while the alloy’s inherent repassivation capability partially restores the protective film. This dynamic interplay modulates the coupled response such that wear damage is enhanced relative to a wear‐only baseline, but the corrosion depth is somewhat mitigated relative to a corrosion‐only baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a uniform, self-forming passive oxide layer that provides initial protection under static, benign conditions.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled sliding wear in a corrosive electrolyte environment.
generation.conditions: Experiments under well-defined laboratory conditions with fixed load, sliding speed, temperature, and electrolyte composition, including parallel tests with wear-only (in inert electrolyte) and corrosion-only (static immersion) to isolate contributions.
generation.structural_mediator: The native passive oxide film that is subject to mechanical removal and subsequent rapid reformation.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear intermittently disrupts the protective oxide film, exposing reactive metal surfaces that undergo accelerated corrosion. In response, the alloy’s corrosion‐resistant elements drive rapid repassivation of the exposed areas. The continuous cycle of film removal and reformation couples the wear and corrosion processes, resulting in enhanced mechanical degradation alongside a moderated corrosion rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under tribo-corrosion the alloy will exhibit a degradation profile that is not simply the sum of independent wear and corrosion effects: wear-induced material loss will be higher than in wear‐only conditions, while the corrosion depth will be lower than that observed in static corrosion due to partial repassivation. The net degradation may thus differ from additive expectations.
generation.baseline: Samples tested under wear-only conditions (with an inert electrolyte preserving the passive film) and corrosion-only conditions (static immersion allowing undisturbed oxide formation).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold when the alloy’s repassivation kinetics are sufficient to reform the passive film under moderate wear. It may not apply in environments with extremely high mechanical loads that overwhelm repassivation or in highly aggressive electrolytes that prevent oxide reformation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise balance between mechanical damage and repassivation kinetics, as well as the quantitative magnitude of the modulation in corrosion depth, remains uncertain and may depend on the specific alloy system and test parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel experiments on identical HEA samples: (1) under tribo-corrosion conditions (controlled sliding wear in a corrosive electrolyte), (2) under wear-only conditions (same mechanical sliding in an inert electrolyte), and (3) under corrosion-only conditions (static immersion in the corrosive electrolyte). Monitor the surface film evolution in situ and perform post-test analyses.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess the integrity and reformation kinetics of the passive oxide film
Surface profilometry and weight loss measurements to quantify wear damage
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to determine corrosion rates
Surface spectroscopy (XPS) to analyze oxide film composition and thickness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tribo-corrosion condition does not show a degradation profile that deviates from the simple additive effects of wear-only and corrosion-only – in particular, if there is no evidence of cyclic oxide film removal and repassivation (i.e., similar film characteristics and corrosion rates as the corrosion-only baseline) and if wear damage is not enhanced – then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys under tribo-corrosion, the coupled degradation is governed by a dynamic interplay between wear-induced removal and rapid reformation of a protective passive oxide film that mediates both wear and corrosion processes.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy exhibiting a stable, native passive oxide film formed under static conditions.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled sliding wear in a corrosive electrolyte environment.
drafts.conditions: Constant sliding speed and load in a fixed electrolyte composition at ambient temperature, ensuring reproducible tribological and electrochemical environments.
drafts.structural_mediator: The passive oxide film that forms on the alloy surface.
drafts.mechanism: During sliding, mechanical wear intermittently disrupts the passive film, exposing fresh metal that rapidly reoxidizes in the electrolyte. This cyclical removal and reformation of the oxide film modulates the corrosion kinetics and wear damage. The film’s self-healing behavior limits corrosion damage, while its periodic removal influences wear, resulting in a coupled degradation behavior where the protective reformation mitigates some corrosion even as mechanical wear occurs.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to a static condition baseline (no sliding), the worn alloy is expected to show a lower corrosion component due to rapid re-passivation, though wear damage may appear slightly enhanced due to continuous film removal. Overall, if the reformation is efficient, the total degradation rate (combined wear and corrosion) should be lower than expected from a simple additive effect of wear and corrosion.
drafts.baseline: An identical high-entropy alloy maintained in a corrosive electrolyte without applied sliding wear, allowing full development and stability of its native passive oxide film.
drafts.boundary: This prediction should hold in environments where the corrosion kinetics support rapid oxide film reformation and the wear rate is moderate. It may fail in highly aggressive electrolytes that disrupt oxide film formation or at extremely high wear conditions where mechanical removal overwhelms the healing rate.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel experiments: one set of high-entropy alloy samples in a corrosive electrolyte under static conditions to establish a baseline, and another set under identical corrosive conditions subjected to controlled sliding wear. Monitor the surface film dynamics and measure both wear and corrosion rates.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to monitor changes in passive film resistance and reformation kinetics
Surface profilometry and weight loss analysis to quantify wear rates
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to analyze oxide film composition and thickness before and after wear
In situ optical or electron microscopy for surface morphology observations during wear-corrosion cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the worn samples do not exhibit evidence of rapid oxide reformation (as indicated by similar film characteristics to the static samples) or if the corrosion damage is not mitigated—as measured by electrochemical and weight loss data—in the presence of mechanical wear, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The coupled tribo-corrosion response in high-entropy alloys is governed by a dynamic process in which mechanical wear intermittently removes a protective passive oxide that, due to segregation of corrosion‐resistant elements, rapidly reforms (repassivation). This continuous cycle partially shields the metal from accelerated electrochemical degradation while simultaneously permitting wear-driven material removal.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a uniform, self-forming passive oxide layer enriched in corrosion‐resistant elements (e.g., Cr, Al) prior to exposure.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy to a controlled sliding wear test in a corrosive electrolyte and compare with matched conditions that isolate only wear (e.g., in an inert electrolyte) and only corrosion (static immersion) respectively.
drafts.conditions: Room temperature; constant load sliding wear under well-defined contact conditions; corrosive solution with controlled pH; and identical alloy microstructure and composition prior to testing.
drafts.structural_mediator: The continuously regenerating passive oxide film whose integrity depends on the segregation of specific alloying elements that form stable oxides.
drafts.mechanism: Mechanical wear intermittently removes the protective passive film, exposing the underlying metal to corrosion. However, the alloy’s intrinsic ability to rapidly repassivate—through the diffusion and segregation of corrosion‐resistant elements—restores the protective layer, effectively coupling and balancing the wear and corrosion processes.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline sample exposed only to pure corrosion or pure wear, the alloy under combined tribo-corrosion should exhibit a reduced corrosion depth (due to repassivation on exposed areas) but an accelerated mechanical degradation profile along the wear tracks. Overall degradation will differ from the simple additive effects of wear and corrosion, showing a unique, moderated corrosion component alongside wear-induced material loss.
drafts.baseline: High-entropy alloy samples subjected to either wear-only in an inert environment or corrosion-only in static immersion, where no repassivation impact from concurrent wear is present.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold when the alloy’s repassivation kinetics are robust and the wear rate is moderate enough to allow oxide film reformation. In cases where the wear rate is exceedingly high or where the alloy composition does not support rapid repassivation, the protective effect might vanish.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel experiments on the high-entropy alloy: (1) under tribo-corrosion conditions (wear in a corrosive electrolyte), (2) wear-only (in an inert electrolyte), and (3) corrosion-only (static immersion in the corrosive electrolyte). Assess the evolution of the oxide film over set time intervals and quantify mechanical and electrochemical degradation rates.
measurements: Oxide film thickness and composition (using XPS or EDX)
Wear track depth and morphology (using profilometry and SEM)
Corrosion rates (using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization)
Microstructural analysis (using TEM) to detect segregation of corrosion-resistant elements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tribo-corrosion samples do not show evidence of a cyclic oxide film removal and reformation (e.g., no enrichment of corrosion-resistant oxides) and their degradation rates approximate the simple summation of wear-only and corrosion-only rates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) under tribo-corrosion conditions, the dominant governing mechanism is the mechanically induced removal of the native, passivating oxide film (which is maintained by selective alloying elements) that normally protects against corrosion. This removal exposes fresh reactive sites that accelerate local corrosion, which in turn roughens the surface and exacerbates wear, creating a synergistic feedback loop.
drafts.material_initial_state: An HEA with a homogeneous distribution of passivating elements and an intact, native oxide film established during exposure to a benign environment.
drafts.intervention: Subjecting the HEA to a combined regime of mechanical wear (e.g., sliding contact under defined load and speed) simultaneously with exposure to a corrosive medium (e.g., salty aqueous solution).
drafts.conditions: Controlled laboratory conditions where wear and corrosion environments can be independently and jointly applied. The comparison would involve samples undergoing the combined tribo-corrosion regime versus samples experiencing wear only and corrosion only, with other factors (temperature, load, electrolyte composition) held constant.
drafts.structural_mediator: The integrity of the surface passive oxide film and its localized mechanical removal.
drafts.mechanism: Mechanical wear causes micro-scale removal or damage of the protective oxide film, exposing unpassivated base metal regions that corrode more rapidly. The corrosion attack then further degrades the mechanical surface integrity, intensifying wear, thereby forming a synergistic loop that increases total degradation beyond the additive effects of separate wear and corrosion processes.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under tribo-corrosion, total degradation (measured by mass loss, surface roughness, and depth of attack) will be significantly higher than in either wear-only or corrosion-only conditions. Both the wear and corrosion components will be enhanced relative to a baseline condition where the passive film remains largely intact.
drafts.baseline: HEA samples exposed individually to wear only (under inert or non-corrosive conditions) and corrosion only (with no mechanical stress), where the passive oxide film remains largely undisturbed.
drafts.boundary: This prediction should hold in environments where the passive film is the primary defense against corrosion and can be mechanically disrupted. It might fail or show less synergy in HEAs engineered with second-phase particles or self-healing oxides that can rapidly reform a protective film even during wear.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled study with HEA samples subjected to (a) wear only, (b) corrosion only, and (c) combined tribo-corrosion. Use identical environmental parameters (load, sliding speed, electrolyte composition, temperature). Monitor the formation and integrity of the passive film in real time using in-situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and post-test surface analysis (e.g., XPS, SEM). Compare the degradation rates (mass loss, surface roughness, pit depth) across conditions.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess passive film integrity
Mass loss measurements
Surface roughness and wear track depth via profilometry or SEM
XPS analysis for oxide film composition and thickness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined tribo-corrosion condition does not yield a significantly higher degradation rate (measured as an increase in both wear and corrosion indicators) compared to the sum of the contributions from wear-only and corrosion-only conditions, or if in-situ measurements show that the passive film remains intact despite mechanical wear, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys under tribo-corrosion conditions, a dynamically forming mixed oxide film serves as a protective mediator that couples wear and corrosion processes. Repeated mechanical removal of the oxide layer is counteracted by corrosion-driven film regeneration, resulting in a net reduction of degradation.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a near-homogeneous microstructure and standard distribution of oxidation‐active elements (e.g., Cr, Mn) as obtained from conventional processing.
drafts.intervention: Modify the alloy by reducing (or contrastively, enhancing) the content of elements that promote stable mixed oxide formation, or apply a surface treatment that inhibits oxide regeneration.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted under controlled sliding wear conditions in a corrosive environment (for example, a saltwater solution) with defined load, speed, and temperature.
drafts.structural_mediator: A mixed protective oxide film composed of corrosion products (e.g., Cr- and Mn-oxides) that continuously forms and heals on the alloy's surface.
drafts.mechanism: During sliding, mechanical wear removes the existing oxide film. Concurrently, exposure to the corrosive environment triggers the formation of a new, adherent oxide layer. The balance between the rate of oxide film removal (due to wear) and its regeneration (via corrosion kinetics) governs the overall tribo-corrosion response.
drafts.predicted_outcome: An alloy variant capable of rapid and robust oxide film regeneration will exhibit lower total degradation (i.e., reduced wear loss and lower corrosion rate) compared to a matched baseline lacking enhanced oxide-forming capability. Under moderate wear and corrosion conditions, this dynamic equilibrium should manifest as a net protective effect. However, if the wear intensity exceeds the regeneration rate, degradation will increase.
drafts.baseline: The standard high-entropy alloy with typical oxide-forming element content and without modifications aimed at altering oxide regeneration.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesized benefit should hold under moderate sliding and corrosive conditions. Under extreme mechanical loading or in highly aggressive corrosive environments where the oxide film cannot regenerate quickly enough, the mechanism may fail to impart significant protection, resulting in similar or enhanced degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with the standard alloy composition and one with either a reduced ability to form protective oxides (via compositional adjustment or a surface treatment) or enhanced oxide-forming capability. Subject both sets to identical tribo-corrosion tests under controlled conditions (fixed applied load, sliding speed, and corrosive medium concentration) for a defined duration.
measurements: Surface analysis (XPS or Auger spectroscopy) to assess oxide film composition and thickness over time
Wear track analysis (SEM, profilometry) to measure mechanical wear loss
Electrochemical measurements (electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and weight loss testing) to quantify corrosion rates
In-situ observation of film regeneration (if feasible)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, despite significant differences in the capacity for oxide film formation, both sample sets show statistically equivalent total degradation, wear loss, and corrosion rates, then the hypothesis that a dynamically forming mixed oxide film is the governing mediator of the coupled tribo-corrosion response would be falsified.
